opus-5.5.text:
Sensing is one of the most underappreciated parts of the problem. When people judge how hard a robotic task is, they tend to focus on the motion: how fast the arm has to move, how many joints, how precise the trajectory. But very often the real bottleneck is perception. It's knowing exactly where things are and what state they're in.

I like to break it down into three sources of uncertainty. There's uncertainty in control: the motors don't do exactly what you command. There's uncertainty in physics: friction, mass distribution, how an object will slide or tumble. And there's uncertainty in perception: the cameras and sensors give you a noisy, partial picture of the world. That last one compounds everything else. If you don't know precisely where an object is, or what its shape is on the side you can't see, then even a perfect controller will fail.

Take something as simple as picking up a glass of water. For a human it's trivial. For a robot, the glass is transparent, so depth cameras basically see right through it. There may be reflections. You don't know how full it is, so you don't know the weight or the center of mass. Suddenly a task that looks easy becomes very hard, and the difficulty is almost entirely in sensing.

Or consider folding laundry. A crumpled shirt has essentially infinite degrees of freedom, and much of it is occluded by itself. Just figuring out what configuration the cloth is in is a huge challenge, before you even think about how to grasp it.

So when I assess a task, I ask: How structured is the environment? Are the objects known in advance, rigid, opaque, and well lit? Or are they novel, deformable, shiny, transparent, cluttered? A factory line, where parts arrive in a known position and orientation, has removed most of the sensing problem by design. That's why industrial robots have worked for decades. Bring the same robot into a home, where nothing is where you expect, and the sensing burden explodes.

This connects to Moravec's paradox: what's hard for humans, like chess or calculus, is relatively easy for computers, and what's easy for humans, like perceiving and manipulating everyday objects, is extraordinarily hard. We have hundreds of millions of years of evolution behind our perception and our sense of touch. Our fingertips are remarkably sensitive, and robots still have nothing close to that tactile sensing.

So I'd say sensing difficulty should be weighted very heavily, arguably as much as anything else. When someone shows a slick robot demo, one of the first questions I ask is how much of the environment was controlled. Were the objects placed carefully? Was the lighting set up? Were there markers? Often the impressive part is the motion, but the part that would break in the real world is the perception. That gap is a big reason I'm skeptical of claims that general-purpose home robots are right around the corner.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes perception uncertainty from control and physics uncertainty, and says sensing difficulty should weigh heavily when assessing a robotic task.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss robotic surgery or a patient's bodily movement as a source of perceptual difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
I think sensing is actually one of the most underrated parts of the whole picture. When people imagine a robot doing a task, they tend to focus on the motion, the arm moving, the hand grasping. But before any of that happens, the robot has to perceive where things are, what they are, and what state they're in. And that's where a huge amount of the difficulty lives.

So when I assess how hard a task is, I'm asking: how much does success depend on perception, and how forgiving is the task when perception is wrong? Take a factory assembly line. The parts arrive in known positions, the lighting is controlled, the objects are rigid and identical. You can almost sense nothing and still succeed. That's why robots have been doing that for fifty years. Now move to a home kitchen. Objects are cluttered, they occlude each other, they're transparent, or shiny, or deformable like a towel or a bag of lettuce. The lighting changes through the day. Suddenly the robot has to resolve enormous uncertainty just to figure out what it's dealing with, and small errors in that perception compound into failed grasps or knocked-over glasses.

So I'd frame it with a few questions. First, how structured is the environment? Second, how much uncertainty is there in the sensing, and is it in the objects, the positions, the materials? Third, and this is the subtle one, how much does the task tolerate error? Picking up a brick, you can be off by a centimeter and it's fine. Inserting a connector or threading a needle, a millimeter matters, and your cameras may not even give you that precision. In those cases you often have to lean on touch or force feedback to close the loop, because vision alone won't do it.

That's one reason I've always been a bit skeptical of the "robots will do everything in five years" claims. The physical world is extraordinarily messy, and perception under that messiness is a hard, unsolved problem. The better frame is to look at where sensing is tractable and build from there, rather than assume it's a solved input to the motion problem.

r001.rationale: The response treats perception and sensing as a major, distinct source of task difficulty, discussing environmental structure, sensing uncertainty, and tolerance for perceptual error.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss robotic surgery or a patient's ongoing bodily movement as a source of perceptual difficulty.

astra-6.text:
I think it should factor in very heavily. When we look at a task, we tend to focus on the motion: how many joints have to move, how precisely, how quickly. But that can obscure the harder question, which is: what does the robot actually know about the world?

If you know exactly where an object is, and you know its shape and its physical properties, then you can often plan a motion to manipulate it. But now imagine that the object is partly hidden, or it’s transparent, or it’s something deformable like a piece of clothing. Even deciding what state it’s in can be difficult. And when you touch it, that state changes.

So two tasks that look almost identical to a person can have very different levels of difficulty for a robot. Picking up a part from a fixture in a factory is quite different from picking up that same part from a pile of other parts. The arm motion may be similar, but the uncertainty is much greater.

And sensing and action aren’t really separate. Sometimes you need to move to get a better view, or touch something to find out where it is. So I would assess the whole loop: what can you observe, what remains uncertain, and can you still act reliably with that uncertainty?

r001.rationale: The response says task difficulty should account heavily for what the robot can know about the world, including uncertainty from hidden, transparent, or deformable objects, and distinguishes this from motion difficulty.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention robotic surgery or a patient's ongoing bodily movement as a source of perceptual difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should factor in enormously. When we describe a task, we tend to describe the physical action: pick up a glass, fold a shirt, open a door. But that description leaves out a lot of the difficulty. Where exactly is the glass? Is it transparent? Is something blocking our view? How much does it weigh, and is it going to slip when we grasp it?

So I’d be cautious about ranking tasks just by how complicated the motion looks. A robot can perform a very precise motion in a factory because the environment has been arranged so that the relevant objects are in predictable positions. A seemingly simpler task in somebody’s kitchen can be much harder because the robot has to figure out what’s going on before it can act.

And sensing and action aren’t really separate. Sometimes you have to act to get information — move your camera, touch an object, or lift it slightly to see whether you have a good grasp. So the question is not just, “Can the robot execute this movement?” It’s, “Can it get enough information to choose a useful action, and recover when its understanding turns out to be wrong?”

r001.rationale: The response says sensing the environment should factor in enormously and explains that perception adds difficulty beyond the physical action itself.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention robotic surgery or a patient's ongoing bodily movement as a source of perceptual difficulty.
